title: Who really needs a cocktail robot?
teaser: Is the Bartesian $300 cocktail robot worth it? It simplifies fancy drinks with capsules and spirits, but taste tests reveal potential artificiality.
summary: The Bartesian cocktail maker functions like a Keurig or Nespresso machine for alcoholic beverages. Users add their own spirits to the Duet model (which supports up to four types of liquor) and slot in specialized capsules containing hyper-concentrated mixes for cocktails like mai tais and margaritas. The device scans capsule barcodes to determine necessary spirits, allowing users to craft drinks at home with minimal effort. While useful for large parties or coworking spaces, the $300 initial cost and repetitive capsule expenses (around $2.50 each) raise questions about its practicality. Reviewers note that some drinks tasted artificial compared to real mixology standards, suggesting it might appeal most to casual party hosts rather than serious cocktail enthusiasts.
author: Amanda Silberling
content: Bartesian's cocktail makers would be best described like a Keurig or Nespresso machine, but for alcoholic drinks. The Bartesian Duet model that I tested certainly lives up to that description - it's really easy to serve a bunch of different cocktails with the push of a button, plus your own liquor. But as I sipped on my raspberry ginger gimlet, I couldn't shake the nagging question: Who is actually going to buy a $300 cocktail robot? There's nothing wrong with the product. And it does exactly what it says! In the sleekly designed machine, you add your spirits of choice (between one and four types of liquor, depending on which model you're using) and plop in a Bartesian capsule with hyper-concentrated mixes for multi-ingredient drinks like espresso martinis, watermelon margaritas, mai tais, and cosmos. There's a barcode on the capsule that your machine scans to determine which spirit (or spirits) you need in your drink, and then you can select how strong you want your drink to be, which modulates the amount of water the machine will use to dilute the concentrate. Then, you put the drink in the provided, high-quality cocktail shaker with some ice to cool it down before pouring it into your glass. When I invited some friends over to test the Bartesian, we enjoyed the inherent novelty of trying out a product we'd never seen or used before. Once we all sat down with our various drinks, we tried to decide who actually makes up the target audience for such an odd product, which also requires the purchase of cocktail capsules at about $2.50 each. Image Credits: Bartesian The Bartesian is not for true cocktail lovers - the capsules don't actually contain any alcohol, which means that if you're making a drink like an aviation, you're getting some sort of non-alcoholic approximation of ingredients like crème de violette and maraschino liqueur. It's no coincidence that my friends and I all liked the Bartesian's lemon drop capsules the best, since the only alcoholic ingredient in the drink is the vodka that we bought ourselves to add to the machine. To be fair to Bartesian, it's not like you'd recommend a Nespresso machine to your friend who owns a Fellow kettle and only buys single-origin beans. This cocktail robot is also not for anyone who is even remotely worried about the amount of counter space in their kitchen. It's pretty big for something that you (hopefully?) aren't using on a daily basis, and if anything, it would probably encourage me to start drinking more often just to justify the $300 expense. Plus, if you have counter space to spare, you probably have a lot of money. And if you have a lot of money and like cocktails, I'd say you are more likely to have a fully stocked bar with fancy liqueurs already. What will the other partners at your law firm say if you serve aviations that don't use real crème de violette? Even as someone who thinks Tito's is top-shelf liquor (I am not that fancy), I could tell that something tasted a little bit artificial about most of these drinks. My friends and I all doctored up our drinks with some seltzer and lemon juice, which made them taste much better. But this kind of post-robot mixing sort of defeats the point of the whole endeavor. Maybe my tastes just don't align with the mixologists at Bartesian - my colleague Lauren reviewed a different Bartesian unit last year and told me that she loved it , especially the margaritas. Drink preferences aside, I still keep coming back to the same question: Who is this product for? I could see the Bartesian being useful if you host a lot of parties and don't hire a bartender, since you can make a whole cocktail menu's worth of drinks without much effort or planning. One friend remarked that this machine feels like the sort of thing that an older couple would keep in their beach house to impress their friends. A colleague suggested that this could really shine in a retirement home. Personally, I could see a Bartesian at a coworking space's happy hour, where people are just happy to get free drinks... then again, there's a reason why WeWork stopped offering unlimited beer back in the day.

title: Instagram introduces a redesigned wordmark
teaser: Instagram updated its wordmark logo, sparking user jokes that the new design actually reads "Instagzam."
summary: Instagram unveiled a redesigned wordmark logo, announcing the change because the previous text-only version felt dated after ten years. Instagram head Adam Mosseri described the updated look as "sharper and more modern." The new design incorporates semi-cursive elements into the typeface for letters like 's,' 'r,' and 'g.' While some users express appreciation for the refreshed aesthetic, others have jokingly noted that the font choice makes it resemble "Instagzam." This change follows Instagram's last major redesign in 2016.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Instagram on Thursday introduced a new wordmark, which is the text-only logo that spells out the company's name. The social media giant's logic was that the older version of its logo felt dated after a decade in use. The change was announced by Instagram head Adam Mosseri on both Instagram and Threads, where he described the new logo as "sharper and more modern" while still referencing the original and maintaining simplicity. Although people can often be averse to change, particularly when it comes to brands and the logos they've long been familiar with, Instagram's refreshed design is seeing some compliments among the complaints, noting the fresher look or praising the font choice. Screenshot Image Credits: Threads While there are certainly plenty of people joking that the logo now looks like it reads "Instagzam" because of the shape of the font used for the "r," it's fair to say that the name "Instagram" is such a recognizable brand that most people will immediately know what this says, despite the artistic flourishes. The wordmark's font recalls cursive writing as it adds old-fashioned curves to the "s," "r," and "g," too. This is something of an interesting choice, given that the younger generations are no longer learning to write in cursive for the most part, so may not immediately understand why the shape that looks like the sail on a little boat is actually an "s." The last time Instagram updated its design was 2016 , when the company moved away from the classic brown camera with the rainbow stripe to the colorful pink gradient that remains the icon today. Meta hasn't yet responded to a request for further comment about the redesign, or whether or not we should expect other design changes to come to Instagram in time, like a new app icon.

title: I finally found a robot lawnmower I’d trust with my yard
teaser: High-tech robot mowers are revolutionizing yard work, but buyers must weigh impressive RTK precision against persistent issues like tangled cables and gate access.
summary: Robot lawnmowers have significantly improved in consistency and maneuverability, making them a viable option for yard maintenance. Key technological upgrades include network Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) navigation—which uses satellite data down to centimeter accuracy—and fallback systems like lidar or vSLAM that allow mowers to keep tracking when GPS signals drop. While the technology excels at tasks like creating consistent lawn lines and handling rough terrain, limitations persist: they struggle with obstacles like garden hoses, extension cords, and reliably detecting cars, and owners must still manually manage property gates for full coverage. The review tested top-tier models including the Husqvarna 420 IQ ($3,299), Mammotion Luba 3 AWD 3000 ($2,799), Navimow X430 ($2,499), and Dreame A3 AWD Pro 2500 ($3,099.99). The Segway Navimow X430 was highlighted as the best performer, successfully navigating challenging transitions and covering ground twice as fast as competitors due to its combined RTK, vSLAM, and vision-based navigation system.
author: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy
content: Robot lawnmowers are finally good enough to take a lot of work out of maintaining a yard, but they're still not set-it-and-forget-it machines. If you don't want these autonomous cutting machines to tear up your lawn or go roaming in your neighbors' yard, you're still going to need to keep an eye on them. But with some oversight, they can take a big chore off your hands. This summer I tested five bots on my flat, three-quarter-acre, coastal South Carolina property with sandy soil, centipede grass, and lots of trees. Things went much better than last year's trials and tribulations , thanks to huge improvements in navigation and maneuverability. Basically, they stopped getting stuck. My lawn has never looked better, and my spouse - who had sworn off robot lawnmowers after a user-error injury - is now a convert. His riding lawnmower has been idle for over a month. The consistency of robot mowers is impressive. Running daily and shaving just millimeters at a time, these mowers have created a noticeably lusher lawn. I walked out on it barefoot this morning - something I've never done before. The best part is that they work quietly around the clock, without bothering my pets, the wildlife, or the neighbors. I also love the professional-looking lawn lines they make. My backyard has mostly been a dry, sandy, dusty landscape with patchy grass. Three months of robot lawnmowers have helped it look healthier. My chickens don't appreciate the neat lines, but I do. The key upgrades this year are network RTK navigation , fallback navigation systems, and improved all-wheel-drive to tackle rougher terrain. RTK - real-time kinematic positioning - is the satellite positioning tech most automowers switched to over the last few years as they've ditched boundary wires. It uses stationary ground-based reference stations (antennas), along with GPS, to provide very precise location data, down to a centimeter or two. It's used for surveying, drone navigation, and anything that needs that fine level of precision. Every mower I tested, apart from the Lidar-based Dreame, comes with its own RTK antenna that needs to be installed in your yard with a clear view of the sky; trees, a neighbor's house, or your own roofline can all block the signal. In my previous testing, I didn't get a single RTK mower to run successfully in my backyard, where I have very spotty GPS coverage. This graphic shows how antenna-based RTK works versus network RTK. Image: Mammotion This new crop all now offers NetRTK as an option. This taps into a network of existing RTK reference stations through a cloud connection, and requires a Wi-Fi or 4G connection on the mower. Most worked out of the box without me needing to install the antenna, but you'll need to check if your house is covered, as coverage varies . RTK mowers now also use a secondary navigation tech such as lidar or vSLAM to keep on track when the signal drops. This improvement in navigation, plus bigger, more capable machines, meant I no longer spent my summer dragging confused mowers out from under oak trees. 1/2 After a few days, the Mammotion had torn up most of this section of damper-than-normal lawn next to my neighbors' yard. However, automowers are far from perfect. These are autonomous machines with blades, and leaving them to their own devices comes with risks. One spent three days methodically destroying a patch of my lawn before I noticed. Another took out two outdoor extension cords. Several models dug sandpits in bare patches, and another tried to climb up a small tree. Obstacle detection is better across the board, but it still has a long way to go. Hoses, cables, and cars are still a challenge - my family now knows to check under the wheels before driving away. No one has really solved gates yet, either (although they're trying ) - I still have to manually open mine to let the robot mow the full property. And, while every manufacturer currently advertises NetRTK coverage as free for the lifetime of the device, there are obvious downsides to relying on a cloud service to mow your lawn. Finally, automowers are still expensive, and I have concerns around long-term durability. Obstacle avoidance is much better, but they still can't reliably see cars. Like their siblings, robot vacuums, there are myriad models on the market now; the right one for you will depend on the size of your yard and your landscape. To find the mower that worked best for me, I tested four top-of-the-line models with specs capable of tackling my challenging terrain and large expanse of my backyard: The Husqvarna 420 IQ ($3,299), Mammotion Luba 3 AWD 3000 ($2,799), Navimow X430 ($2,499), and the Dreame A3 AWD Pro 2500 ($3,099.99). I also tried the entry-level Roborock RockNeo Q110H ($1,299) on my front lawn, which is more like a standard suburban lawn. Also like robot vacuums, robot lawnmowers fall under the new FCC robot ban , so while existing models can continue to be sold and supported in the US - including all the models reviewed here - the fate of new models is in question. The robot I'd get for my yard $2499 Navigation : RTK, vSLAM / Yard size : up to 1 acre / Cutting : 0.75" to 4" height, 17" width (dual discs) / Terrain capabilities : 4WD, zero-turn wheels, 84% slope / Theft features : Lift and out-of-zone alarms, GPS anti-theft, PIN / Weatherproofing : IP67 / Connectivity : 4G (1 yr free then $32.90 a yr), Wi-Fi, BLE / Warranty : 3 yrs Read More The Segway Navimow X430 ($2,499) is by far the best mower I tested. This 60-pound beast looks like Darth Vader's dog, and was the only mower I tested that didn't get stuck once. Its 4WD wheels combined with impressive suspension rolled through the potholes, over sticks and rocks, even small tree branches. It navigated around my chickens and across the tall, uneven transition from my front yard to back yards - it was the only bot that could mow both in one trip (with the gate open). It uses a combination of RTK, vSLAM, and vision-based tech to navigate, and it covered my entire property without once getting lost or stuck. It features impressive "xero-turn" maneuverability enabling it to pivot smoothly with no lawn damage. Its dual-disc, 17-inch cutting width covers more ground, and it was able to mow most of my backyard in under three hours - nearly twice as fast as most competitors. I really liked the remote-control mowing feature, which was handy for tidying up the edges of the lawn and more sensitive areas such as around flower beds. The Segway's speed does mean a few blades go untrimmed, and its rain sensing relies on weather data from the internet, which meant it often didn't mow because it predicted rain that never came. Setting up the NetRTK was a bit tricky, mostly because I had to put the charging station in an awkward spot to connect to the GPS (it can't be under an awning or up against a building as the mower also needs a clear view of the sky). A good lidar-based alternative $2500 Navigation : Lidar, AI vision (camera-based) / Yard size : 0.62 acre / Cutting : 1.2" to 3.9" height, 15.8" width (dual discs) / Terrain capabilities : AWD, zero-turn wheels, 80% slope / Theft features : Lift and out-of zone alarms, GPS anti-theft, PIN / Weatherproofing : IPX6 / Connectivity : 4G (3 yrs free), Wi-Fi, BLE / Warranty : 2 yrs Read More The Dreame A3 AWD Pro 2500 ($3,099.99) is the best option if you can't rely on RTK. Its lidar and camera-based navigation performed nearly as well as the Segway in my backyard, only getting stuck a couple of times. It doesn't need a clear view of the sky, so you can place it anywhere, and its sliding edge-cutting deck worked slightly better than the Segway's EdgeSense feature in my testing. (Beware, it's set to a fixed 1.2-inch minimum). But in my testing, lidar was the least reliable navigation tech, and sometimes the A3 declared the job complete when it wasn't. Lidar robots do best in a fenced-in yard, as they can more easily get lost and wander off into your neighbors' yard, something that never happened with the RTK robots. While the Dreame rarely got stuck, its turning mechanism wasn't as smooth as the Segway, and it dug several sandpits in various spots where there was no grass. I do like its "Garden Guardian" mode that uses the camera as a roaming security guard, and it can also identify when people cross its path and warn them that it's working. It's been mildly hilarious watching it surprise the heck out of dog walkers passing by the front yard. An expensive but reliable option for yards with no trees $3144 Navigation : EPOS (RTK), radar / Yard size : 1 acre / Cutting : 1" to 4" height, 9.4" width (single discs) / Terrain capabilitie s: 2WD, large wheels, 45% slope / Theft features : Out-of zone alarm, GPS anti-theft, PIN / Weatherproofing : IPX5 / Connectivity : 4G (free for life), Wi-Fi, BLE / Warranty : 4 yr mower, 3 yr battery Read More Husqvarna's Automower 420 IQ ($3,299) is a good option for a standard yard. It has the longest warranty (four years), the easiest app and controls, and a modular design for longevity. It's 2WD, but its large wheels tackled uneven terrain well. It requires an RTK antenna and has the option of cloud-based RTK (in some areas), but its backup navigation for satellite dead spots requires installing physical boundary wire. I tested this in my neighbor's yard using the physical RTK antenna, as they have fewer trees and clearer views of the sky. It navigated well, but it uses radar for obstacle detection and has no camera at all. This meant it wasn't as good at dodging objects as the others, and ran into the bushes once and tried to climb a small tree. The Husqvarna mowing my neighbors' lawn - I had to install it there as the RTK antenna didn't work in my yard. There is the option of netRTK. But if you have a large, uncomplicated, tree-free yard, it's a good option thanks to Husqvarna's broad support network, free-for-life cellular connectivity for both theft and NetRTK (should you need it), and impressive performance. More reliable navigation, but spotty software $2239 Navigation : Lidar, RTK, AI-vision (camera-based) / Yard size : 0.75 acre / Cutting : 1" to 2.7" height, 15.7" width (dual discs) / Terrain capabilities : AWD, 80% slope / Theft features: Lift and out-of zone alarms, GPS anti-theft, physical key / Weatherproofing : IPX6 / Connectivity : 4G (3 yrs free), Wi-Fi, BLE / Warranty : 3 yrs Read More The Mammotion combines all three wireless navigation types - RTK, lidar, and vision - making it ideal for properties with spotty GPS coverage like mine. But it's less nimble than the other AWD models thanks to lower ground clearance and weaker suspension. While the Mammotion did great cutting the lawn, it had serious issues with turns and soft ground. It dug itself sandpits and tore up grass in a particularly soft spot. Its turning mechanism also tore up a couple areas of my garden, particularly a shaded area near my neighbors' sprinklers, which stayed damper than other spots. Mammotion has acknowledged this issue, telling The Verge "We've identified that a recent update to the turning logic caused some unwanted results. The mower turning too sharply might tear up the grass to some extent, especially when the ground is wet and slippery, or the grass isn't very thick." They've deployed several software updates to address this, but we should all be wary of relying on software updates to fix fundamental problems with an expensive lawnmower. A budget option for smaller yards with or without trees $1000 Navigation : RTK, vSLAM / Yard size : 0.25 acre / Cutting : 0.8" to 2.4" height, 8.7" width (single disc) / Terrain capabilities : 2WD, 45% slope / Theft features : Out-of zone alarm, GPS anti-theft (with optional module), PIN / Weatherproofing : IPX6 / Connectivity : Wi-Fi, BLE (4G sold separately) / Warranty : 2 yr Read More The $1,299 Roborock RockNeo Q110H is my budget pick. This rear-wheel-drive mower was impressive on my flat, treed front yard, although its lack of all-wheel-drive meant that the occasional large tree root stopped it in its tracks. That, and its more limited range, is why it's half the price of other mowers here. It offers RTK and vSLAM navigation, with the option of antenna or NetRTK. The RockNeo is remarkably similar to the Segway Navimow i100N I tested last year, with a few upgrades, including better camera-based obstacle detection, steeper slope navigation (up to 45%), and a wider cutting blade. It can also be used for manual remote-control mowing and has a built-in edge-cutting feature, although there's the option of an edge-cutting add-on module, which I haven't tried. Edge cutting is still very much a work in progress for all mowers. Some do well straddling the edge, but if you have a fence or delicate boundary, that won't work. Companies are trying all sorts of solutions - including special attachments. Ecovacs Goat A3000 Pro Lidar looks to be the most promising, thanks to a side-mounted string trimmer. But for now, you should plan to keep your manual trimmer handy. The Segway mowing the backyard. Robot mowers have improved significantly over the last 18 months. Advances in navigation have solved my main pain points from my last round of testing , and bigger, beefier bots are now better at navigating the varied terrain of American yards. Today, the right bot will maintain your yard beautifully with minimal effort. While they still need oversight and the occasional rescue, and they haven't solved every problem, they do take a lot of the work out of maintaining your yard. title: Give Google the boot by building your own search engine
teaser: Tired of Google? An open-source tool lets you build your own niche search engine for specific web content using minimal resources.
summary: Alex Morley-Finch developed Marlin, an open-source project that allows users to build highly focused search indexes bypassing the scope of major engines like Google. Built with low overhead—costing only around $10 in cloud GPU time and less than a gigabyte of storage—Marlin's goal is indexing specific content types (like portfolios or art projects). The system uses four processes, including a fetcher and a worker connected to a local language model for summarizing pages. Morley-Finch implemented a weighting system to focus the crawl on desired areas rather than broadly scanning the internet. However, he notes that relying on an LLM for categorization led to '671 distinct categories' and over 121,000 tags, suggesting the design is suited for hobbyist projects but may struggle with large-scale implementation.
content: software Give Google the boot by building your own search engine Got $10 and a gig of storage space? Marlin lets you weight your crawl toward the parts of the web you actually care about If you're fed up with search results drowning out the bits of the web you actually care about, you could always build your own search index, as one developer did. Nottingham, UK-based software dev Alex Morley-Finch built the open-source project dubbed Marlin for himself, cataloging around 560,000 homepages for roughly $10 in rented cloud GPU time and using less than a gigabyte of disk storage. Morley-Finch said in a writeup of the project that he wanted a search engine of things he cared about, like "portfolios, zines, weird little art projects, one-person software," and other cases of just "people doing stuff" that they share on the internet. Something simple, with "a crawler that only ever looks at homepages, a small local language model that reads each one and writes a name, two or three sentences, a category, and a handful of tags," he explained. "No IP scanning, no Redis, no storing full page HTML, no recrawl scheduler, nothing multi-tenant." Morley-Finch built Marlin around four processes: A fetcher that grabs domains, a worker that makes calls to a small, OpenAI-compatible language model, a steward that prevents bad pages from making their way into the index, and an API with a web UI where he can track the process and actually conduct searches of his index, complete with filters. Of course, you can't expect something like this to go perfectly on the first try. "The first version worked within a couple hours. Point it at a sample of domains, watch things get summarised, search for them. Great," he said in his writeup of the project. "Sunday afternoon [he began working on Marlin on a Sunday], I looked at what had actually been catalogued and it was the wrong web." Instead of indexing what he wanted it to, Marlin had just been grabbing a cross section of the internet, leading to more than 90 percent of the first attempt being "corporate sites and documentation." Rather than blocking certain domains, Morley-Finch built a weighting system to push certain pages to the top of his crawl queue, and others as far down the list as possible. Morley-Finch rented a cloud GPU to handle most of the heavy processing and stopped the crawl at around 560,000 pages after exhausting his prioritized categories and beginning to pull in "the raw internet." He spent around $10 on the cloud GPU. The one overarching problem he had, and which he said may be a problem for anyone else who tries to replicate his project, is tagging and categorizing - left to a language model, those important elements got a bit messy. "I let the model invent its own category and tag names freely, on the theory that it would teach me the taxonomy instead of me guessing one upfront," he explained, noting that it helped things get started quickly, but "I ended up with 671 distinct categories, many used exactly once, and over 121,000 tags, more than half used only a single time." Morley-Finch had to build a manual merge tool to clean up the mess, leading him to declare that his design likely won't scale well beyond a hobbyist project, as "'just let the model freestyle' catches up with you fast." Still, he reckons Marlin's rough edges shouldn't put off anyone willing to spend a weekend tinkering with it. "I think this is very doable in a weekend, and cheap enough that the GPU bill isn't the reason not to try," Morley-Finch wrote. "The code is going up as open source, so you can point your own crawl wherever your own curiosity leads." The Marlin GitHub repo is filled with how-tos and details for those who want to create their own weighting list based on their priorities, with the option to rent a cloud GPU if their hardware isn't up to the challenge. ®

title: Everything is better with pickles... except Windows
teaser: Windows tech malfunctions even during an ad break: A PC link error popped up at Wendy's.
summary: A software malfunction was spotted on a Windows ad screen at Wendy's featuring the 'Windows Phone Link' app. This service is designed to link a PC to mobile devices (Android/iPhone), allowing users to manage calls and notifications from their desktop. The glitch indicates issues with stack memory—possibly due to a conflict or shortage—requiring a simple restart. While its function is minor, this public failure highlights how easily system connections can fail.
content: offbeat Everything is better with pickles... except Windows Operating system indigestion pops up over chicken sandwich ad BORK!BORK!BORK! "Everything is better with pickles," trumpets a Wendy's sign. Everything is also better with a helping of bork, if the screen is to be believed. Do you want bork with that? Spotted by an eagle-eyed Register reader in Vancouver, the display shows something amiss with Windows Phone Link - although why a PC encouraging customers to drop dollars on a Dill Pickle Chicken Sandwich needs the app is anyone's guess. The error itself usually comes up when something running Windows has been a bit careless with stack memory. Perhaps there's been a stack overflow, a software conflict, or a memory shortage. The usual fix is to reach for the power button or perform a restart. The more technically minded might try to diagnose the whoopsie and fix it without a boot cycle, although had a more technically minded person set up the system in the first place, it's unlikely that the PhoneExperienceHost.exe application would have reared its ugly head in this way. Phone Link connects a Windows PC to an Android phone or iPhone. The theory goes that users can keep track of mobile notifications, send and receive messages, or deal with calls from their Windows desktop. It arrived with Windows 10 as Your Phone before Microsoft renamed it Phone Link and continued adding features. Ordinarily, the service doesn't use much in the way of memory or CPU. However, something has clearly upset the instance here, much as an excess of dill pickles might disagree with the customer. While we're sure the foodstuffs on offer are excellent (although our reader told us they were only popping in for a Frosty Dairy Dessert rather than anything slapped with a dill pickle), we might give the chicken sandwich a miss this time. Even Windows appears less than keen. ®
